analysis.one_liner: Requires warrants before the government can search Americans' communications collected under foreign-surveillance law.
analysis.headline: The USA RIGHTS Act drew 26 bipartisan House sponsors but never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the foreign-surveillance law known as Section 702 of FISA. It would have required a warrant before government workers could search the emails and calls of Americans swept up in foreign-targeting surveillance, banned collecting purely domestic communications, and barred using that surveillance data against people in ordinary court cases. It also would have strengthened outside oversight of the secret FISA court and extended the underlying surveillance authority for four more years as the trade-off.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans whose phone and internet communications can be swept into foreign-surveillance collections. Warrant and query limits would shield their messages from warrantless government searches, and use restrictions would keep that data out of ordinary criminal and civil cases against them. Journalists, lawyers, and others who routinely contact people overseas would gain a path to sue in court. Internet and phone companies would gain clearer, court-checked limits on what assistance the government can compel and stronger rights to publish statistics about surveillance orders.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary Americans using phones and email

how_it_helps.text: Requires a warrant before federal officers can query surveillance collections for the communications of a U.S. person or anyone inside the United States, with narrow emergency exceptions, ending so-called backdoor searches of Americans' messages.
Bars the government from acquiring communications known to be entirely domestic, or communications involving no targeted person, under foreign-targeting surveillance authority.

Prohibits using surveillance-collected information about Americans as evidence or in investigations in ordinary criminal, civil, or administrative cases, except for national-security threats like terrorism or espionage approved by the Attorney General.
Gives people who reasonably believe their communications will be collected and who take reasonable steps to avoid surveillance the standing to challenge the program's constitutionality in court.

Requires the secret FISA court to approve any technical assistance demanded of communications providers, ensuring it is necessary, narrowly tailored, and not an undue burden, and expands what providers can publicly report about surveillance orders they receive.

Strengthens independent oversight by expanding the Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board's mandate and whistleblower channels, adding court advocates (amici) with broader access to argue for privacy in FISA court proceedings, and requiring declassification and public statistics about surveillance.

analysis.who_pays: The main cost falls on the intelligence community and federal law enforcement, chiefly the NSA and FBI, which would lose warrantless access to Americans' communications in surveillance databases and face new court checks and reporting. Federal prosecutors would lose a source of evidence in ordinary cases. Communications providers would face compliance requirements for court-approved assistance and transparency reporting. Taxpayers fund the expanded oversight apparatus.
analysis.who_pays_short: Intelligence agencies and federal law enforcement

drawbacks.text: The bill extends the FISA Amendments Act of 2008 — the legal basis for bulk foreign-targeting surveillance — by four years, to September 30, 2021, so it would lock in the underlying surveillance authority even while restricting it.

The protections are not absolute: the Attorney General can approve using surveillance-derived information in national-security proceedings, and corporations are exempted from the warrantless-query prohibition entirely.

Only people with a reasonable basis to believe they are targeted and who took objectively reasonable steps to avoid surveillance can sue, which leaves most Americans without a practical way to challenge the program in court.

The bill leaves the core of foreign-intelligence targeting intact: surveillance of non-Americans abroad still requires no individualized warrant, so the government's overall collection of foreign communications continues.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy gains for Americans are substantial and concrete — warrant-backed protection of their messages from government database searches, court-checked demands on providers, and real oversight of a secret court. The honest cost is that the bill trades those protections for a four-year extension of the surveillance authority itself, and its exceptions for the Attorney General and for corporations soften the edges. It is a meaningful but partial reform, not an end to the program.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to four House committees, passed down to two subcommittees, and never got a committee markup or a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Zoe Lofgren and six original cosponsors from both parties introduced the bill on October 25, 2017, as the Section 702 surveillance authority approached its scheduled expiration.

The bill was referred to four committees at once — Judiciary, Intelligence, Oversight and Government Reform, and Homeland Security — a multi-committee referral that gives any of them control over the bill's fate.
It was further referred to subcommittees on November 1 and November 14, 2017, and the action record ends there: no hearings, no markup, no vote, and no floor action for the rest of the Congress.
The bill included its own four-year extension of the 2008 FISA Amendments Act through September 30, 2021, positioning itself as the reform bargain in the reauthorization debate.

Cosponsorship grew to 25 members — 16 Republicans and 9 Democrats — including both libertarian-leaning and progressive members, but the bill never received a vote of any kind before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The intelligence agencies and House leadership who wanted surveillance powers renewed without these restrictions came out ahead: the underlying authority was reauthorized separately that same Congress with far fewer protections, and the warrant and use restrictions proposed here never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Intelligence agencies and the surveillance status quo

sides.party_line_note: Support was genuinely bipartisan — 16 Republicans and 9 Democrats cosponsored — but since no committee or floor vote ever happened, the party split on the merits was never tested; the blockage came from the Republican majority's leadership and committee chairs.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped agencies of warrantless searches for Americans' communications in surveillance databases and barred most courtroom uses of that data. Its interest in continued unchecked access runs against the public's privacy.

industries.industry: Internet and communications providers (tech companies, telecoms)
industries.note: Providers would get court-checked limits on compelled surveillance assistance, freedom from demands deemed an undue burden, and much broader rights to publish how many surveillance orders they receive. Their gain aligns with customers' privacy interest.

The bill reshapes the court with new judge-selection rules, public counsel (amici) with access to argue privacy concerns, and required declassification of major decisions, while also keeping the court as the gatekeeper for surveillance approvals.
